strengths: Novel mechanistic insight: Demonstrates that self-supervised speech models implicitly encode articulatory structure through strong linear mapping to EMG power (r=0.85), with compelling explanation for why HuBERT layer 6 is optimal for downstream tasks

Comprehensive analysis: Thorough layer-wise evaluation across multiple SS models (WAV2VEC 2.0, HuBERT, WavLM) with consistent patterns, effectively demonstrating the articulatory-representation relationship

Dataset advancement: Contributes a significantly larger EMG corpus (9 hours, 6,800+ unique words, 115 WPM natural speaking rate) compared to prior work (1,024 words, 45-78 WPM), addressing data scarcity in the field
Methodologically grounded: Uses theoretically motivated approaches (SPD covariance matrices, geodesic distances) with careful experimental protocol and thorough preprocessing documentation
Clear presentation: Well-written with informative visualizations (electrode placement, gesture clustering) and detailed methodology sections supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Substantially incomplete evaluation (Critical): Section 6 explicitly states core evaluation methods are 'currently exploring' and 'developing,' including WER, CER, and perceptual quality assessment. A speech synthesis paper without these fundamental metrics or audio samples/listening tests is unfinished. This indicates submission of ongoing work rather than completed contribution

High error rates without quality validation: Best performance shows 41.42% PER without audio samples, MOS scores, or listening tests. Impossible to assess whether synthesized speech is intelligible or practically useful, undermining the entire end-to-end system

Severely limited generalization evaluation: Only 12 participants for gesture analysis; main synthesis corpus appears single-speaker (unclear from ambiguous singular 'subject' references throughout). No cross-subject evaluation, transfer learning, or generalization analysis. This fundamentally undermines claims about broader applicability

Confusing experimental structure: Gesture dataset (Section 5.1) collected 'independently' from main corpus (Section 3); unclear whether synthesis results use same or different speakers. Ambiguous statements about subject count make replication difficult

Unjustified reduction from vec(E) to D(E): Substituting D(E) ∈ ℝ²² for vec(E) ∈ ℝ⁹⁹¹ to avoid ill-posedness (footnote 4), then claiming findings support nonlinear inverse problem lacks justification. Tables 1-2 show vec(E) significantly outperforms D(E), suggesting D(E) misses important structure
No code or data available yet: Promised 'upon completion of project' with no timeline. Prevents community validation and reproducibility despite claimed commitment to openness
Limited multi-speaker evaluation and no transfer learning: Despite emphasizing few-shot/zero-shot learning as a key benefit (Introduction), provides no evidence of transfer across speakers or domains

Incomplete system analysis: No ablations on Rotation-Invariance module; minimal hyperparameter details (learning rates, convergence); no failure mode analysis; vocoder limitations not discussed; greedy decoding used instead of beam search
Weak comparison with prior work: No direct quantitative comparison with methods [2,6] using same metrics. Comparison limited to dataset size and experimental setup rather than actual performance

Temporal stability and drift not addressed: Linear correlation r=0.85 derived from controlled gesture data; unclear if holds in conversational speech. No analysis of electrode drift over time/sessions or long-term stability

Scope mismatch for ACL: Core contribution is EMG signal processing and speech synthesis (more suited to Interspeech/ICASSP). While SS model interpretability is interesting, it is secondary to system performance
Missing fundamental metrics for speech synthesis: No WER, CER, or audio quality evaluation makes it impossible to contextualize the 41% PER error or assess practical utility compared to prior work

strengths: Novel analysis of relationship between EMG covariance matrices and self-supervised speech representations, demonstrating linear mapping with r=0.85 across multiple models
Significant dataset contribution: ~9 hours of EMG data with 6,800+ unique words at natural speaking rate (~115 wpm), substantially improving upon prior work limited to 1,024 words at 45-78 wpm
Principled mechanistic insight explaining why HuBERT layer 6 is optimal for speech resynthesis through its maximal capture of articulatory structure
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple self-supervised models (HuBERT, wav2vec 2.0, WavLM) and layer depths with clear visualizations
Interpretable approach grounding EMG feature design in articulatory mechanisms and covariance-based representations rather than black-box learning
Clear problem formulation addressing the challenging alignment-free setting without prior knowledge of EMG-speech synchronization
weaknesses: CRITICAL: Incomplete primary contribution—paper claims 'end-to-end EMG-to-speech synthesis' but provides no perceptual or objective audio quality evaluation (MOS, WER/CER on synthesized output). Section 6 acknowledges perceptual quality assessment as 'continuing work,' making core claims unverifiable

Single-subject evaluation for synthesis task (Section 5.3) with no cross-subject generalization testing; unclear subject count is inconsistent with gesture study (12 subjects). For clinical applications, this severely limits validity

Methodological compromise: Direct H→vec(E) probing abandoned as ill-posed; substitution with D(E) (22-dim projection) was post-hoc and weakens claims about full articulatory encoding. Inverse problem acknowledged as ill-posed but success not explained mechanistically

No performance comparison with prior EMG-to-speech work [2,6]. Without baselines, UER=58.7% and PER=41.42% cannot be interpreted as competitive. Different datasets complicate comparison, but even relative difficulty assessment is missing

Limited novelty for NLP venue: HuBERT/wav2vec application is straightforward; TDS architecture borrowed from prior work [21]; EMG covariance matrices are standard signal processing; pipeline follows prior work [2,6]. Paper reads as biomedical/signal processing application rather than NLP contribution

Incomplete reproducibility: data/code promised 'upon project completion' (Footnote 2) but project incomplete (Section 6). Missing hyperparameter selection details, ablation studies, training procedures, and optimization specifics

Missing error analysis and ablations: no explanation for why vec(E)>D(E)>vec(B); no phoneme-level performance breakdown; no analysis of failure modes or challenging articulatory gestures; no ablation on TDS architecture choices

Presentation and scope issues: key limitations in footnotes; 'continuing work' section reveals incompleteness inappropriate for submission; no dedicated discussion section; claimed zero-shot/few-shot capabilities never evaluated despite being introduced as motivation

strengths: Novel mechanistic insight: demonstrates that SS speech models (particularly layer 6) implicitly encode articulatory mechanisms through strong linear mapping to EMG power (r=0.85), providing principled explanation for why this layer is optimal for downstream tasks

Valuable dataset contribution: creates large-vocabulary EMG corpus (~9 hours, 6,800+ unique words) at natural speaking rates (~115 wpm), directly addressing critical limitations of prior work (which used <1,024 words at 45-78 wpm)

Principled EMG feature representation: uses symmetric positive definite (SPD) covariance matrices with geodesic distance, theoretically grounded approach that naturally captures articulatory structure (70.6% clustering accuracy for D(E), 73.7% for full E)
Comprehensive SS model analysis: systematic layer-wise evaluation across HuBERT, wav2vec 2.0, and WavLM variants reveals consistent patterns in how different models capture articulatory information

Clear presentation and visualization: well-motivated writing with effective figures (t-SNE clustering, layer-wise correlations) that clearly communicate the relationship between EMG, SS representations, and articulatory gestures
Practical non-invasive approach: addresses broader population than invasive BCIs, with applicability to laryngectomy, dysarthria, and dysphonia
weaknesses: Critical gap: end-to-end synthesis evaluation is incomplete. Paper reports phoneme error rate (41.42%) and unit error rate (58.7%) but lacks perceptual quality metrics, word error rates, character error rates, and speech intelligibility scores—all essential for a speech synthesis paper. Section 6 acknowledges these are 'currently being developed' rather than presented, undermining the main synthesis claim

Limited subject analysis: gesture study uses 12 participants, but main speech synthesis corpus appears single-subject (adapted from prior work [3]). No cross-subject evaluation, subject-independent models, or generalization analysis provided—severely limits practical applicability claims

No quantitative comparison with prior work: cites EMG-to-speech systems [6,7,8] but provides no head-to-head evaluation on comparable metrics. Claims to address prior limitations (vocabulary size, alignment-free setting, speaking rate) but offers no evidence of actual performance improvement

Contradictory results weaken emphasis on D(E): Figure 3 emphasizes strong H→D(E) mapping (r=0.85), yet Table 1 shows vec(E) substantially outperforms D(E) for synthesis (58.7% vs 62.96% UER). This gap—suggesting full covariance captures important information missed by diagonal—deserves deeper analysis but is left unexplored

Methodological circularity in linear probing: uses D(E) as proxy precisely because it encodes articulatory structure, then uses this to argue H encodes articulatory information. Direct vec(E) probing would be more convincing, though ill-posed

Missing critical experimental details and ablations: no justification for 100 discrete units from layer 6, no ablation of Rotation-Invariance module or TDS architecture, no phoneme-level error analysis, no sensitivity to hyperparameters. Test set appears intra-subject split rather than subject-independent
Data availability unclear: promise to release 'upon completion of the project' is too vague; timing and access conditions undefined, limiting reproducibility

Incomplete error analysis: no breakdown by phoneme, speaking rate, sentence length, or vocabulary frequency. No analysis of which discrete units are confused. No assessment of alignment quality in alignment-free setting
Vocoder domain mismatch not addressed: Tacotron trained on standard speech must convert EMG-derived discrete units—potential distribution shift not discussed or analyzed
Borderline fit for ACL: paper is primarily signal processing/neuromuscular interface work with limited NLP/linguistic components; discrete unit prediction is present but not deeply explored

strengths: Significant dataset contribution: publishes one of the largest EMG-to-speech datasets (9 hours, 6,800+ unique words from healthy participant; 1 hour from ALS participant), enabling reproducibility and future research

Novel analysis of EMG-S3 relationship: well-motivated discovery that D(E) maps linearly to HuBERT representations (r=0.85) with layer-wise analysis explaining why layer 6 is optimal for downstream tasks
Alignment-free learning: addresses realistic clinical scenarios (degraded audio, laryngectomy) without assuming temporal EMG-audio alignment, unlike prior benchmarks

Reproducible methodology: extensive implementation details in appendices, clear experimental protocols, human evaluation with multiple raters, ablation studies on training data effects, commitment to releasing code/data
Phoneme-guided decoding: principled approach using articulatory structure to improve unit decoding by 9% absolute UER (56.08%→51.81%), grounded in speech production theory
Comprehensive evaluation: multiple metrics (UER, PER, WER, MOS), human transcription validation, ablation studies, and interpretable covariance-based features make findings transparent
weaknesses: Critical methodological issue: healthy participant trained on synthetic Google Text-to-Speech audio, not subject-recorded speech, creating unacknowledged distribution mismatch; this core design choice buried in footnote rather than prominently disclosed; undermines clinical relevance claims

Severely limited clinical validation: single ALS participant with only ~1 hour of data; no longitudinal evaluation, no assessment of robustness to distribution shifts (electrode placement, impedance, disease progression), no comparison of non-stationarity vs. invasive BCIs

No generalization evidence: single healthy participant with no cross-subject evaluation, transfer learning experiments, or inter-subject variability analysis; unclear if approach generalizes beyond specific individuals

Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing components (TDS from Sivakumar et al., HuBERT units, Tacotron vocoder); covariance-based EMG features are principled but not novel; seq2seq inverse mapping is standard nonlinear technique

No direct method comparison: authors acknowledge lack of compatible baselines; different alignment assumptions and training targets make WER comparisons to Gaddy & Klein (42%), Littlejohn et al. (74%), Metzger et al. (54%) unreliable and potentially misleading

Performance far from clinical deployment: WER of 62.55% (healthy) and 50.82% (ALS) remain substantially higher than invasive BCIs; MOS of 3.79 indicates moderate quality; improvements from phoneme-guided decoding still leave system impractical

Linear mapping analysis uses low-dimensional proxy: H→D(E) uses only 31-dim representation instead of full 961-dim vec(E); justification for why D(E) is fundamentally better than spectrograms (r=0.85 vs r=0.57) lacks mechanistic explanation; information bottleneck not rigorously analyzed

Incomplete human evaluation: only 3 raters for 460 sentences (no inter-rater reliability reported); high variance in ALS WER (±1.59%); MOS evaluated on only 35/460 test sentences; no objective spectral distance metrics comparing to natural speech

Inadequate ablation studies: loss weights appear arbitrary (λ_unit=0.8, λ_phone=0.1, λ_cons=0.1) without justification; no ablation on context length (25ms seems short for coarticulation); phoneme-guided decoding mechanism not mechanistically explained

Signal quality and preprocessing concerns: self-paced mouse-clicking for timing could introduce artifacts; no signal quality metrics or noise analysis; minimal preprocessing (only bandpass filtering) without artifact removal or electrode impedance discussion

strengths: Large-scale, publicly released EMG datasets (9 hours healthy, 1 hour ALS) address reproducibility issues in prior work
Novel finding that self-supervised speech representations (HuBERT layer 6) correlate strongly with EMG power (r=0.85), providing mechanistic insight into articulatory encoding
Principled articulatory foundation: covariance-based EMG features naturally cluster by gesture type (61-74% k-medoids accuracy)
Comprehensive experimental methodology with multiple evaluation metrics, human transcription by 3 raters, ablations, and statistical reporting over 5 seeds
Non-invasive approach demonstrated on real ALS participant using silent articulation, addressing scenarios where invasive BCIs are not suitable
Detailed implementation reporting and promised open-source release support reproducibility
weaknesses: Venue mismatch (critical): Paper is speech signal processing and biomedical engineering work, not computational linguistics/NLP. Core contribution doesn't address language structure, understanding, or generation. ACL 2026 scope is computational linguistics, not signal processing.

Severely limited clinical validation: Only 1 ALS participant with 1 hour of data; no longitudinal studies, no assessment of distribution shift over time or disease progression. Claims about clinical applicability (laryngectomy, dysarthria, dysphonia) unsupported by single case study.

Circular evaluation methodology and text supervision confound: HuBERT targets derived from Google text-to-speech (not ground-truth subject speech). Model learns EMG → text-derived representations, not purely EMG → speech. Text transcripts at training time confound signal processing contribution.

Incomparable evaluation to prior work: 62% WER on unaligned setting with 6,800-word vocabulary, vs. Gaddy & Klein (2021) 42% WER on aligned setting with smaller vocab. Different alignment assumptions, corpora, vocoders, and text supervision levels make it impossible to assess actual progress. Authors decline direct benchmarking.

Single healthy participant with no cross-subject evaluation or transfer learning assessment. Linear scaling with training data (Figure 7) indicates model is data-limited and generalization to new speakers is unclear.

Reliance on strong pretrained models obscures EMG contribution: HuBERT (trained on massive corpus), Tacotron vocoder, Google TTS, and phoneme mappings provide strong priors. Simple linear mapping H→D(E) already achieves r=0.85; unclear how much additional non-linearity TDS encoder learns.

Linear probing analysis uses D(E) (31-dim) as proxy for vec(E) (961-dim), losing information. Full vec(E)→speech mapping would be more ill-posed than linear probing suggests. Overstates linearity of H→EMG relationship.

Missing ablations: TDS architecture adapted from keyboard typing domain; generalization to continuous speech unexplored. Necessity of shift-tolerant module not ablated. No comparison of EMG-only vs. EMG+text supervision.

Silent vs. overt articulation modes not distinguished: Healthy participant used overt speech, ALS participant used silent articulation. Different motor control patterns likely; transferability of phoneme-guided decoding across modes unvalidated.

EMG covariance window size and temporal alignment for continuous speech unclear; only 1.5s gesture windows specified. High sensitivity of covariance features to electrode placement (acknowledged) problematic for clinical deployment.
Phoneme-guided decoding learned on healthy (overt) participant data and transferred to ALS (silent) participant without validation of cross-mode transfer.
MOS evaluation limited to 35 sentences (7.6% of test set). MOS=3.79 could reflect vocoder quality masking poor EMG input; vocoder may hallucinate plausible speech even with corrupted HuBERT units.

No direct comparisons: Only brief mention of EMG2QWERTY baseline; no comparison to other seq2seq architectures or standard EMG signal processing. Appendix C BCI comparisons explicitly not intended as direct comparisons.

strengths: Excellent reproducibility and open science practices: open-sourced dataset (one of largest EMG-to-speech resources), complete code, detailed hyperparameters, enabling community advancement

Novel empirical contribution establishing quantitative linear relationship between S3 speech representations and EMG power (r=0.85), providing mechanistic explanation for why HuBERT layer 6 is optimal for articulatory encoding
Sound technical methodology: well-motivated covariance-based EMG features grounded in articulatory mechanisms, appropriate use of CTC for alignment-free learning in clinically realistic scenarios
Phoneme-guided decoding is creative and well-motivated, achieving meaningful improvements (UER: 56.08%→51.81% healthy, 52.29%→46.98% ALS) by exploiting phonetic structure
Comprehensive human evaluation with 3 independent transcribers, MOS ratings, and ablation studies on training data size showing consistent linear improvements

Significant practical motivation: non-invasive approach more accessible than invasive BCIs, demonstrated on real ALS patient, addressing clinically important populations (laryngectomy, dysarthria, dysphonia)
Interpretable design: covariance features and phoneme-unit mappings (Figure 6) meaningfully connected to speech production regularities rather than black-box approaches
weaknesses: Critical limitation: only 2 participants (1 healthy, 1 ALS) with ~1 hour ALS data; cannot assess cross-participant generalization, day-to-day variability, electrode placement sensitivity, or long-term stability—fundamental requirements for clinical prosthesis claims

Moderate performance relative to invasive alternatives (62.55% WER vs. 54% for Metzger et al. 2023 with invasive electrodes; 43% for Wairagkar et al. 2025); performance gap limits near-term clinical utility

EMG2TEXT (51.17% WER) substantially outperforms proposed EMG2SPEECH (61.02% WER), suggesting direct synthesis task is fundamentally constrained or approach leaves significant room for improvement—raises questions about method choice

Limited architectural novelty: adapts existing TDS model from Sivakumar et al. (2024); phoneme-guided decoding is relatively straightforward consistency regularization; relies entirely on pretrained HuBERT and Tacotron

Insufficient ablation studies: covariance matrix choice not compared against other interpretable alternatives; shift-tolerant module not ablated; design hyperparameters (λ weights) not justified; no analysis of which muscle sites matter for phonetic categories

Experimental design using gTTS targets instead of subject's own audio introduces acoustic mismatch, particularly for healthy participant where original audio exists but is unused for synthesis—complicates interpretation of performance

No longitudinal validation: missing study of performance stability over days/weeks despite non-invasive interfaces typically being less stable than invasive alternatives—critical gap for prosthesis deployment claims

Moderate statistical rigor: only 3 human raters for WER (no inter-rater reliability metrics reported); MOS from only 35 sentences, 10 raters; no significance testing between feature representations (Table 1); results remain single-participant studies

Scope and generalization: all English speakers, cannot evaluate language/age/disease-state variation; silent articulation for ALS differs fundamentally from vocalized speech; linear mapping (Section 5.2) shown only on healthy participant

Limited relevance to core NLP: paper is primarily signal processing and speech synthesis engineering; while touching articulatory phonology, may be better suited for speech/biomedical engineering venues than ACL
